fields.meta_title: Contractor Landing Page Builder for Estimates | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a contractor landing page that asks for the project and budget, then books the walk-through. Four builder and remodeler examples.
fields.h1: Build a Contractor Landing Page That Books Estimates
fields.hero_description: Get a contractor landing page that turns project requests into estimate visits, each request saved to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Remodeling Request Page Needs
fields.features_subheading: Six parts take a homeowner from a rough idea to a request your estimator can price, and Emergent changes each one by prompt.
fields.feature_1:
The project type comes first

Start with fixed choices: Kitchen, Bathroom, Basement, Addition, or Whole home. One tap answers it, and the choice tells the office which estimator should read the request.
fields.feature_2:
A start date to plan around

Ask when work should begin: within 3 months, in 3 to 6 months, or still planning. A job that starts next month gets a call this week, and a planning lead can wait a few days.
fields.feature_3:
The job address near the top

Ask for the street and city early in the form. The estimator sees the drive before reading the scope and can price a request from across the county with the travel time in mind.
fields.feature_4:
A row for every request you get

Each submission becomes a row in a database you own, holding the project type plus the minute it arrived. Your office marks the row Visited, then Estimate sent, as the job moves.
fields.feature_5:
An email or a Slack post

Send each new request to the estimator by email, to an office Slack channel, or to both. The message carries the homeowner's phone number and the project type for the first call.
fields.feature_6:
A web address from your yard signs

Publish the page on a domain you already own, such as an estimates subdomain of the site printed on your yard signs. Custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits.

fields.tab_content_1:
Site walks go to Ruth when the budget hits $75,000

Ostrander Pell Builders asks for a budget range before the address. A request at $75,000 or more emails Ruth Calloway, the owner, who books the site walk herself. Anything below goes to Dario Fenn, the estimator, for a phone estimate first. This month 31 requests came in: 9 went to Ruth and 22 to Dario.
fields.tab_content_2:
Tuesday and Thursday mornings, booked on the page

Fennick Remodeling puts the estimator's open mornings on the page: Tuesday at 9 am or Thursday at 9 am. The homeowner picks one while sending the request, and each booking emails Teodor Lindqvist, the estimator, with the job address. This week 14 walk-throughs were booked, 8 on Tuesday and 6 on Thursday.
fields.tab_content_3:
Gallery photos that open a filled-in form

Harrow Lane Kitchens & Baths shows its finished rooms before it asks for anything. Under each photo, a button opens the estimate form with that room already picked. A visitor who liked the walnut kitchen starts on Kitchen. Last month 40 requests came in: 26 started from a gallery photo and 14 from the plain form.
fields.tab_content_4:
The past client's name rides on every referral

Wexcombe Construction wrote a page for past clients to pass along to friends and neighbors. The form asks who sent the visitor, and each request emails Marisol Quint, the office manager, with that past client's name for a thank-you note. This quarter 12 referral requests came in, naming 7 past clients.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Contractor Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to a contractor landing page that sorts project requests by type and budget and books the estimate visit.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Give each project its own page
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Open the form with the project type
fields.howto_step_1_des: Point the kitchen ad at a kitchen page and the addition ad at an addition page. A homeowner planning a second story wants to see additions you built, not a bathroom tile gallery.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Make the first field a short list of choices instead of an open text box. Put it ahead of the name and the address, because the choice decides which estimator hears about the request.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Mark the phone field as a tel input. MDN notes that it causes mobile browsers to display a special keyboard for entering phone numbers, which saves a homeowner on a ladder some typing.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Resize and compress every project photo before it goes on the page, and check the first screen on a phone. web.dev advises that sites should strive to have Largest Contentful Paint of 2.5 seconds or less.
fields.howto_step_5_des: List three or four ranges with no gaps between them, such as Under $25,000, $25,000 to $75,000, and over $75,000. Keep the top range open-ended, and test the list with two or three past clients before launch.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Tell the homeowner who calls back and when, in the words you would use on the phone: the estimator's first name and the day of the call. Then keep that promise for every request.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Build it and send a test request
fields.howto_step_7_des: Describe the projects, the budget ranges, and who prices each one, and Emergent builds the page from that prompt. Send a test request from a phone, then check the database row and the estimator's email.

faq_plan.q: What is a contractor landing page?
faq_plan.a: A contractor landing page is a single page built for one kind of job, such as kitchen remodels or home additions, that asks the visitor for one thing: an estimate request. It pairs a short form with photos of finished work and leaves the company history and the full service list to the main website.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a contractor landing page?
faq_plan.a: Describe the projects you take, the questions to ask, and who should hear about each request, and Emergent's AI landing page builder turns that description into the page. Publish it on your own domain, then point your ads and truck signs at it.

faq_plan.q: Should a construction landing page show past projects or just a form?
faq_plan.a: Show both: the form first on a phone, and finished projects right below it. Label each photo with the project type and the town, and keep the gallery to the kind of job the page is for. A visitor looking at additions should see additions.

faq_plan.q: Should my ads point to a different contractor landing page than my website?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Give paid clicks their own page: a visitor from an ad for basement finishing should land on a page about basements. Keep the form near the top, with no menu leading off to decks or siding. The guide to the ppc landing page covers the ad side in more depth.

faq_plan.q: What should a contractor landing page ask before the walk-through?
faq_plan.a: Ask for the project type, the start date, a budget range, the job address, and a phone number, and stop there. Leave measurements and finishes for the walk-through, where the estimator can see the room.

faq_plan.q: Should a contractor landing page ask homeowners for a budget?
faq_plan.a: Yes, as a range instead of an open box. Add a line under the question saying the range helps you plan the visit and that the price comes from the estimate itself. That keeps the homeowner from reading the range as a quote.

faq_plan.q: Can a contractor landing page send estimate requests to my CRM?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Apps that Emergent builds connect to any tool with an API, syncing data in and out. Each request can arrive in your CRM as a new contact with the project type and budget range attached. A crm landing page is a different thing: a page that markets CRM software itself.

faq_plan.q: Can homeowners book an estimate visit on a contractor landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Offer the estimator's open windows as choices on the form, and ask for the job address in the same step so the estimator can plan the drive. Emergent builds the page from a plain-English prompt and changes it by prompting. Next week's windows go up with one sentence.

faq_plan.q: Should a contractor landing page list prices for remodeling work?
faq_plan.a: Only for fixed-scope work you sell the same way every time, such as a deck stain or a tub-to-shower swap, where a starting price helps. For full remodels, show the budget ranges you take instead, and let the estimate carry the price.

faq_plan.q: How do I reach commercial clients with a contractor landing page?
faq_plan.a: Build a separate page for commercial work, with project types such as tenant improvements and office build-outs, and ask for the company name and the square footage instead of a home budget. If you reach property managers through paid social, the guide to the linkedin landing page covers that audience.

plan.angle: Searchers for contractor landing page get design galleries (Dribbble, Nicepage, Pinterest, Landdding), one agency service page and a social post that says a landing page should carry one offer and one next step; none of them shows what happens to a remodeling request after the homeowner presses the button. This page shows four general contractor and remodeler pages built around the estimate (a budget range that decides who walks the job, walk-through slots booked on the page, a finished-project gallery that fills in the form, a referral page that records which past client sent the lead), each with the form, the routing and the database row behind it, then gives the build steps. It stays out of HVAC, roofing, licensing, permits and back-office project workflow.
